title: How to Make Wealth
summary: An essay arguing that startups are the reliable route to wealth because they combine measurement (small teams) and leverage (technology), while warning that payoffs are lottery-shaped, luck is large and hard work is the price.

assertions.quote: I think your best bet would be to start or join a startup. That's been a reliable way to get rich for hundreds of years.

verdicts.note: Startups produce many of the self-made fortunes, but most fail and the median founder payoff is near zero, so 'reliable' overstates it.

Incorporated entrepreneurship offers fat-tailed upside (a 90th-percentile entrepreneur earns 30% more than his own earnings as a 90th-percentile employee) with bounded downside since those who quit return to salaried work at their old wage, but only ~0.8% of salaried workers incorporate a year, the gains concentrate in high-skill rule-breakers, and the paper measures hourly earnings, not getting rich; nothing supports 'most reliable'.
Startups produce many self-made fortunes, but most fail and median founder and early-employee payoffs are near zero, so they are high-variance rather than reliable.

assertions.quote: there is not a fixed amount of wealth in the world. You can make more wealth.

verdicts.note: Long-run growth in real output is the standard evidence against zero-sum wealth.

assertions.quote: To get rich you need to get yourself in a situation with two things, measurement and leverage.

verdicts.note: A useful framing consistent with where large fortunes arise, but it is a heuristic rather than a tested model.

assertions.quote: If the mean is 30x, the median is probably zero. Most startups tank

verdicts.note: Venture return data show power-law outcomes with most companies returning nothing to founders.

Entrepreneur earnings are right-skewed: incorporated owners' mean residual hourly earnings are 48% above salaried workers versus 28% at the median (18% vs 6% within-person), but the median is clearly positive, not zero; the paper measures owners' hourly earnings, not startup equity payoffs.

assertions.quote: If you're in a job that feels safe, you are not going to get rich

verdicts.note: Risk-return trade-offs are general; counterexamples exist via long compounding of savings, so it is not absolute.

Incorporated self-employment has fat tails both ways (the 10th-percentile incorporated earns 10% less than his own earnings as a bottom-decile employee, the 90th-percentile 30% more), but the downside is bounded because failed entrepreneurs return to salaried work at essentially their old wage; the paper does not test whether a salaried job can make one rich.

assertions.quote: If starting a startup were easy, everyone would do it.
you need more than that to make as much money as he has. You also need to be very lucky.

verdicts.note: Studies of founder and investor outcomes show large unexplained variance and weak persistence, consistent with a big luck component.

assertions.quote: when you discover a new way to do things, its value is multiplied by all the people who use it

verdicts.note: Scalable products have near-zero marginal cost while services scale with hours; this is why software fortunes dwarf service ones.

assertions.quote: Users are the only real proof that you've created wealth.

verdicts.note: Usage is a strong signal but can be bought or unmonetizable; revenue and retention matter too.

assertions.quote: you should be especially skeptical about any plan that centers on things you like doing

verdicts.note: Passion-driven ventures often misjudge demand, though domain enthusiasm also drives persistence; evidence is mixed.
